newsitem.title: UK: BMA welcomes Labour's plan to raise health spend.
newsitem.headline: BMA welcomes Labour's plan to raise health spend.

text.p: The British Medical Association (BMA) on Wednesday praised Labour's plans to spend an additional 1.2 billion pounds on the National Health Service (NHS) in 1998-1999.
But it urged the government to use receipts from a higher tobacco tax to set up a contingency fund to help hospitals cope with illnesses this winter.

"The government has listened to the distress calls from doctors. The increase for the NHS next year is sufficient to wipe out NHS deficits and give us a fresh start," Dr Sandy Macara, BMA chairman said in a statement.

But he added that the doctors' group wanted to see extra money coming from the tobacco tax, estimated to be 160 million pounds for a full year, allocated to a 'fire fighting fund' to help the health service get through the winter.
As reported, the extra 1.2 billion pounds that Labour plans to allocate to health next year will come out of the government's five billion-pound contingency reserve for 1998-1999.

Economist Julian McCrae of the independent Institute for Fiscal Studies commented that health spending this year still was projected to rise by only 1.8 percent in real terms, or below the average three per cent annual real spending rise for health since 1979.

"He (Chancellor Gordon Brown) hasn't solved the long-term problems," McCrae said, adding that the government still will have to find money in 1999-2000 to match the increase in spending announced for 1998-1999.
